lead: MPI is the Message Passing Interface: a library and standard for programs whose processes have separate memories. They cannot read each other’s variables. To cooperate, one process packs data into a message and sends it; another receives it. This is the natural model for a cluster, where each node has its own RAM, and for supercomputers used in weather, crash simulation and train scheduling. This chapter shows the six calls that carry most MPI programs: init, rank, size, send, receive and finalize, then the collectives that replace many hand-written messages.
prereq: You need: Unit 1’s distributed-memory model and the message-passing basics in Unit 4; compare with shared-memory programming, where threads share variables.

blocks.text: Every MPI program starts with MPI_Init(&argc, &argv) and ends with MPI_Finalize(). Between them the process may call MPI. A communicator is a named group of processes allowed to talk. The default, MPI_COMM_WORLD, contains all processes started by mpirun -np P. P is the number of processes.

Inside a communicator each process has a rank: an integer from 0 to P−1. MPI_Comm_rank(comm, &rank) writes the caller’s rank into rank. MPI_Comm_size(comm, &size) writes the number of processes into size. Rank is an identity, not a priority; rank 0 is usually the root that reads input and prints output.

Each process runs the same program, called SPMD: single program, multiple data. It uses if (rank == 0) ... else ... to take different paths. Variables are private. If rank 0 sets x = 5, rank 1’s x is unchanged unless a message carries the value. This is the key break from Pthreads and OpenMP, where a shared variable is visible to all threads.

sections.h3: Point-to-point: send, receive, tag and deadlock

blocks.text: A point-to-point message has a sender and a receiver. The basic calls are MPI_Send(buf, count, datatype, dest, tag, comm) and MPI_Recv(buf, count, datatype, source, tag, comm, &status). buf is the address of the data; count is how many items; datatype is e.g. MPI_INT or MPI_DOUBLE; dest and source are ranks; tag is an integer label; comm is the communicator. MPI_Recv also needs a status object that records the actual source and tag.

Tags let one process send different kinds of message to the same receiver. A receive with tag 7 will not take a message with tag 8. Source can be MPI_ANY_SOURCE and tag MPI_ANY_TAG, but then read the real values from status.

Both calls are blocking in the usual sense. MPI_Send returns when the send buffer can be reused; for a small message it may copy into an internal buffer and return at once, for a large message it may wait until the matching receive starts. MPI_Recv returns only after the message has arrived and been copied into buf. So a blocking send is not a promise that the receiver has finished using the data.

Deadlock is the common failure. If rank 0 calls MPI_Send to rank 1 and then MPI_Recv from rank 1, while rank 1 calls MPI_Send to rank 0 and then MPI_Recv from rank 0, each send may wait for the other’s receive. No process proceeds. Safe orders: make one side send first and the other receive first, or use non-blocking calls, or MPI_Sendrecv which does both in one call.

A collective is one call made by every process in a communicator. The library does the many point-to-point messages for you. All ranks must pass matching arguments for that collective: same root for rooted collectives such as Bcast, Scatter, Gather and Reduce, same count and datatype, and same op for Reduce. Otherwise the program may hang. If one rank skips a collective, the others wait forever.

head: Collective
Action
rows: Root sends the same buffer to every rank.
Combines each rank's value with an operation such as MPI_SUM into the root's buffer.
Root splits its array into equal chunks, one chunk per rank.
Root collects one chunk from each rank into its array.

blocks.text: Root-worker pattern: rank 0 is root. It reads the whole array, scatters chunks, workers compute local results, reduce returns combined result to root, root prints. Total elements = size × count per rank. In the sum example root sends [5,6,7,8] to rank 1 and keeps [1,2,3,4]; each rank sums; MPI_Reduce with MPI_SUM adds 10 and 26 to give 36 at rank 0. MPI_Gather would instead collect the two local sums [10,26] at root. The figure shows the two-rank case.

figure.caption: Rank 0 scatters the second half [5,6,7,8] to rank 1; rank 1 returns its local sum 26. Rank 0 adds its own local sum 10 to print 36.

spec.aria: Root sends the second half of the array to rank 1; rank 1 returns local sum 26; root adds its own 10 to get 36.

examples.question: Two MPI processes, ranks 0 and 1, sum A = [1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8] with MPI_Scatter and MPI_Reduce using MPI_SUM. Give the four elements and local sum of each rank, and the final sum at rank 0. Write the key MPI calls.
steps: P = 2 processes and n = 8 integers, so each rank gets count = 8 ÷ 2 = 4 elements.
Rank 0 receives indices 0 to 3: values [1,2,3,4]. Local sum = 1+2+3+4 = 10.
Rank 1 receives indices 4 to 7: values [5,6,7,8]. Local sum = 5+6+7+8 = 26.
MPI_Reduce with MPI_SUM sends both local sums to root rank 0. Root computes 10 + 26 = 36.
For printing, MPI_Gather collects [10,26] at rank 0; the final total is already 36.
examples.answer: Rank 0 gets [1,2,3,4] with local sum 10; rank 1 gets [5,6,7,8] with local sum 26; MPI_Reduce gives final sum 36 at rank 0.
examples.check:
A = [1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8]
local0 = A[:4]
local1 = A[4:]
s0 = sum(local0)
s1 = sum(local1)
total = s0 + s1
print(s0)
print(s1)
print(total)

traps: Processes do not share variables. A global array in the program text is a private copy in each process; only messages or collectives move values.
A blocking MPI_Send is not a guarantee of delivery to the receiver's buffer; it only says the send buffer can be reused. Two sends before two receives can deadlock.
Ranks start at 0, so P processes have ranks 0 to P−1. Off-by-one errors in root or dest are common.

Collectives must be called by all ranks in the communicator, with matching arguments for that collective: same root for rooted collectives, same count and datatype, and same op for Reduce. One missing call hangs the job.
MPI_Scatter splits the array; it does not give every rank the whole array. That is MPI_Bcast.

quiz.q: Which call writes the number of processes in a communicator into a variable?
Why does an MPI process not see another process's global variable?
quiz.a: Each process has its own address space; the same program text runs with private data. Values move only in messages or collectives.

quiz.q: P = 4 processes, A has 20 integers, and MPI_Scatter uses count = 5. Which indices does rank 2 receive?
quiz.a: Ranks get blocks: rank 0 indices 0-4, rank 1 indices 5-9, rank 2 indices 10-14, rank 3 indices 15-19. Rank 2 gets A[10] to A[14].

quiz.q: Both ranks call MPI_Send and then MPI_Recv. Explain the deadlock and give one fix.
quiz.a: Each send may block waiting for a matching receive, and no receive has been posted. Fix: rank 0 sends then receives while rank 1 receives then sends, or use MPI_Sendrecv or non-blocking calls.

quiz.q: Which call ends MPI use in a process?
State one difference between MPI_Bcast and MPI_Scatter.
quiz.a: Bcast gives the same full buffer to every rank; Scatter gives a different chunk to each rank.

quiz.q: Local sums 10 and 26 are reduced with MPI_SUM to root. What does root get?
Why must all ranks call MPI_Reduce with the same root and op?
quiz.a: A collective is one global operation; the library matches calls across ranks. A mismatch can hang the job or produce wrong data, so every rank in the communicator must participate with matching arguments.

beyond: Not for the exam. MPI-2 added one-sided communication; MPI-3 added shared-memory windows and non-blocking collectives. Real clusters use MPI under Slurm job scripts, often with GPU-aware MPI so a message can go straight from one GPU to another. Python users meet the same ideas through mpi4py. Search next for one-sided communication (MPI-2), non-blocking collectives (MPI-3), and GPU-aware MPI.
